title: MALICE
mv: Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men.
mvp: “Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men.” 1 Corinthians 14:20
assignment: Think of a situation where someone offended you or treated you unfairly. Using God’s word as a guide, list five factors to let go of malice and walk in love and forgiveness. (2X5=10 marks).

b.x: Malice is more than just avoiding or not talking to someone. It is a behaviour intended to harm people, their reputations, cause embarrassment and upset them. All these often occur because of a hostile impulse or deep-seated meanness. Malice is also the feeling of pleasure at someone’s misfortune, an intentional evil by someone seeking to injure or kill. People feel malice toward those they hate. If someone feels malice toward you, look out! They have bad intentions for you. Ephesians 4:31 instructs believers to put away malice and other harmful behaviours.

i: Cain’s jealousy and malice towards Abel, his brother, led to the first murder recorded in the Bible (Genesis 4:1-8).
The Philistines envied Isaac's increasing wealth and filled the wells his father had dug with dirt; a malicious act intended to drive him away (Genesis 26:14-15).
Esau harboured malice toward Jacob and vowed to kill him because of the blessing he deceitfully received from their father. (Genesis 27:41).
Joseph’s brothers hated him because of his dreams and attempted to kill him (Genesis 37:12-28).
Saul developed a malicious jealousy and fear for David’s sudden popularity and acceptance among the Israelites (1 Samuel 18:6-16).

Shimei, Saul’s relative, cursed King David as he fled Jerusalem, acting with great malice towards the King (2 Samuel 16:5-8). He was later killed by Solomon as a result of malice passed down from David (1 Kings 2:8-9, 36-46).
The Jewish leaders sought to harm Jesus (Matthew 12:14-15; Luke 23:1-25).

b.x: Jesus said ‘malice’ (wickedness), along with other sins, comes from within the heart and makes one unclean (Mark 7:20-23). Therefore, to get rid of malice, do not harbour cruelty in your heart or let your actions be motivated by it (Psalm 28:3; Jeremiah 17:9). You must not seek revenge against those who hurt you (Leviticus 19:18; Romans 12:17). Rather, forgive everyone who hurts you (Matthew 6:14-15, Luke 17:3-4). Embrace the new life devoid of malice in Christ (1 Corinthians 5:8).

Engage in conversation to immediately address issues with the person who has offended you. Refusal to do this is a subtle way malice can take root in your heart and degenerate into terrible and regretful actions.
Make conscious efforts to get rid of malice.

i: Identify four biblical instances of malice.
Mention four practical ways to get rid of malice.
